newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy employers see 97 growth lower, inflation up.
newsitem.headline: Italy employers see 97 growth lower, inflation up.

text.p: Italy's employers association Confindustria said it has revised down its forecast for 1997 gross domestic product (GDP) growth to 1.5 percent from 2.0 percent and sees 1997 average inflation at 3.2 percent.
The forecasts were published in the latest economic study by Confindustria's research office.
The government forecasts 1997 GDP growth at 2.0 percent and average inflation at 2.5 percent.

Confindustria, which confirmed its 1996 GDP growth estimate of 0.7 percent, against a government forecast of 1.2 percent, said the 1997 growth outlook is tied to economic recovery in the rest of Europe.

"In Italy's situation, this is taking place slowly mainly because our monetary policy is tighter than in other countries. Such a policy is partly attributable to the lack of credibility in the convergence of Italy's inflation and public finances towards Maastricht parameters," the report said.
Average 1996 inflation was seen at 3.9 percent, in line with official government forecasts, and the year-on-year rate below 3.0 percent at the end of the year, it said.

But Confindustria warned, "in the following few months it will be difficult for the downward inflation trend to continue... because there will be less impact from the stronger lira seen this year and the consequences of this year's wage rises and labour costs will probably also be felt next year."

Giampaolo Galli, director of the research office, said that in addition to the key 32.4 trillion lire 1997 budget which has to be presented to parliament by September 30, another mini-budget for next year will be needed to keep the deficit within the government's target of 88 trillion lire.
Addressing a Confindustria forum on the economy, he said the employers body feared "there will not be enough cohesion to enforce a rigorous economic policy".

"If the 32.4 trillion lire budget goes through, it is easy to predict that additional budget measures will be needed in the spring, not in order to meet Maastricht criteria but to achieve the weak government targets contained in its three-year rolling target programme (DPEF)," Galli said.
The DPEF sets the 1997 PSBR target at 88.0 trillion lire, or 4.5 percent of GDP.
Galli also forecast an additional key Bank of Italy interest rate cut by the end of this year, after July's reduction in the discount rate to 8.25 percent from 9.0 percent.
"We forecast a half point cut by the end of 1996 but we fear that the easing process will then come to a halt," Galli added.
